title: UK Graduate Visa 2026: Rules, Fees & How to Apply
metaDescription: UK Graduate visa 2026: who can apply, the fee and health surcharge, how long you can stay, what work is allowed — and the changes coming in 2027.
headline: UK Graduate Visa 2026: Rules, Fees & How to Apply

sections.title: What the Graduate Route Gives You
sections.content:
The Graduate visa lets international students stay in the UK and work — or look for work — without needing a sponsoring employer. It is one of the most flexible UK routes: there is no job offer requirement, no salary threshold, no maintenance funds requirement and no English test. Almost any job is allowed, including self-employment and freelance work, with the single exception of professional sport.

Timing matters more than ever. Applications made on or before 31 December 2026 get two years of stay, or three years for PhD graduates. From 1 January 2027, the standard grant drops to 18 months, while PhD graduates keep three years. If you are finishing your course in 2026, the application date decides which rules you get.

sections.title: Who Can Apply
sections.content:
You must apply online from inside the UK, before your Student visa expires — you cannot apply for the Graduate visa from abroad. Your university must have reported your successful course completion to the Home Office before you apply, so check with your institution's immigration team rather than assuming the paperwork is done. Only students who completed an eligible UK degree qualify.

Once granted, you are free to work at any skill level while you look for longer-term sponsorship. But plan ahead: the Graduate visa cannot be extended, and time spent on it does not count toward settlement under the Skilled Worker route — though it may count toward the ten-year long residence route. Many graduates use the time to secure a sponsored Skilled Worker role.

sections.title: Fees and the Immigration Health Surcharge
sections.content:
The application fee is around £937 — note that some older sources still cite £822, so check the current figure on gov.uk before you apply, as fees are updated periodically. On top of that, you pay the Immigration Health Surcharge upfront for the full grant: £1,035 per year, which works out at roughly £2,070 for a two-year visa. The surcharge gives you access to the NHS on broadly the same basis as residents.

Budget for the total before you start the application, because both payments are due when you apply and are generally non-refundable. There is no maintenance requirement — you do not need to show savings — but the upfront cost is real, so factor it into your post-graduation plans alongside rent and living costs.

sections.title: Working on the Graduate Visa
sections.content:
Work rights are deliberately broad. You can take any job at any skill level, switch employers freely, and work as self-employed or freelance. That flexibility is the route's main selling point: it buys you up to two years to build UK experience, grow a professional network and find an employer willing to sponsor you under the Skilled Worker route.

The only notable exclusion is professional sport, including coaching — you cannot work as a professional sportsperson on this visa. Everything else, from graduate schemes to part-time work to running your own business, is permitted. Your employer needs no sponsor licence and faces no extra paperwork, which removes a real barrier when job hunting.

sections.title: Limits, Travel Rules and What's Next
sections.content:
The hard limits: the visa cannot be extended, and time on it does not count toward Skilled Worker settlement — it can, however, count toward the ten-year long residence route. You also cannot travel outside the UK while your application is pending; leaving the Common Travel Area withdraws the application automatically, so stay put until you get a decision, which typically takes around eight weeks.

Dependants need attention too. A new dependant rule for UK-born babies took effect on 3 August 2026, and partners can only join in limited circumstances — the Graduate route is primarily for the graduate themselves. If your long-term plan is settlement, use the Graduate period strategically: it is a bridge to sponsored work, not a destination.

faqs.q: How long does the UK Graduate visa last?
faqs.a: For applications made on or before 31 December 2026, the visa lasts two years — or three years for PhD graduates. From 1 January 2027, the standard grant shortens to 18 months, while PhD graduates keep three years. The length is fixed at grant and the visa cannot be extended, so plan your next immigration step early.

faqs.q: Can I apply for the Graduate visa from outside the UK?
faqs.a: No. You must apply online from inside the UK, before your Student visa expires. Your university must also have reported your successful course completion to the Home Office first. If you have already left the UK or your Student visa has lapsed, you are not eligible — there is no overseas application route.

faqs.q: How much does the UK Graduate visa cost?
faqs.a: The application fee is around £937, though some older sources cite £822 — check gov.uk for the current figure before applying. You also pay the Immigration Health Surcharge upfront at £1,035 per year, roughly £2,070 for a two-year grant. Both payments are due when you apply and are generally non-refundable.

faqs.q: Does the Graduate visa count toward UK settlement?
faqs.a: Time on the Graduate visa does not count toward settlement under the Skilled Worker route, and the visa cannot be extended. It may, however, count toward the ten-year long residence route. Most graduates treat it as a bridge: up to two years of unsponsored work to secure an employer willing to sponsor them.

faqs.q: Can I travel while my Graduate visa application is pending?
faqs.a: No — do not travel outside the UK while your application is pending. Leaving the Common Travel Area automatically withdraws your application. Stay in the UK until you receive a decision, which typically takes around eight weeks. Once the visa is granted, you can travel freely within its validity.
